title: Phishing Awareness
summary: Recognise deceptive messages before they cost you credentials, money or data.
what_is_it: Phishing is a message (email, SMS, chat, social media, QR code or call) that pretends to come from someone you trust so that you click a link, open a file, share credentials or send money.
why_it_matters: Phishing is one of the most common first steps in real-world breaches. One stolen password or one approved payment can be enough for an attacker to get in.
warning_signs: Suspicious sender: the display name says 'IT Helpdesk' but the address is from an unrelated or look-alike domain (for example helpdesk@examp1e.invalid with the digit 1 instead of the letter l).
Urgency or threats: 'Your account will be deleted in 2 hours'.
Credential request: any message asking you to 'confirm' your password or MFA code.
Unexpected attachment: an invoice, voicemail or 'scanned document' you were not expecting, especially .zip, .html, .iso or macro-enabled files.
Suspicious link: the visible text says one site but hovering shows a different address.
Payment request: new bank details, gift cards or 'urgent' wire transfers.
Impersonation: a message that appears to come from a manager, supplier or well-known brand but with an unusual tone or request.
Unexpected QR code: a QR code in an email or on a poster asking you to 'log in' or 'pay'.
safe_practices: Hover over links (or long-press on mobile) to preview the real destination before clicking.
Go to important sites by typing the address or using a saved bookmark, not by clicking links in messages.
Verify unusual requests through a trusted channel you already know (the official phone number, not the one in the message).
Use the 'Report phishing' button so the security team can protect everyone.
Use a password manager - it will not auto-fill your password on a fake site.
what_to_do: Do not click, reply or forward the message to colleagues.
Report it using the official reporting button or to the security team.
If you already clicked or entered a password: change the password from a trusted device, and tell the security team immediately. Speed matters more than embarrassment.

extra_sections.title: Safe practice example (annotated, fictional)
items: Subject: 'URGENT: mailbox full - verify within 1 hour' -> red flag: urgency.
From: 'Mail Admin' <admin@mailbox-verify.invalid> -> red flag: sender domain does not match your organisation.
Body asks you to 'confirm your password' -> red flag: legitimate IT teams never ask for your password.
Correct response: do not click, report the message, and if worried contact IT using the number on the intranet.

title: Password Security
summary: Long, unique passwords stored in a password manager stop most account attacks.
what_is_it: Password security means creating passwords that are hard to guess and never reusing them, so one leak cannot unlock your other accounts.
why_it_matters: Attackers automatically try leaked username/password pairs on many sites ('credential stuffing'). Reused passwords turn one breach into many.
warning_signs: You use the same password (or small variations) on several sites.
Your password is short, a dictionary word, or includes personal details like birthdays.
You receive a 'password changed' notification you did not expect.
A service tells you your password appeared in a known breach.
safe_practices: Use a unique password for every account.
Prefer long passphrases (four or more random words) - length beats complexity.
Use a reputable password manager to generate and store passwords.
Turn on MFA for every account that supports it, starting with email and banking.
Never share passwords, even with IT staff - they will never need it.
what_to_do: If a password may be exposed, change it immediately from a trusted device.
Change it everywhere you reused it.
Check active sessions/devices on the account and sign out unknown ones.
Report work-account concerns to the security team.

extra_sections.title: Why a password manager helps
items: It remembers hundreds of unique passwords so you only remember one strong master passphrase.
It fills passwords only on the real website address, which helps you notice fake login pages.
It can warn you about weak, reused or breached passwords.

title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
summary: A second factor blocks most attacks that rely on a stolen password.
what_is_it: MFA requires something you know (password) plus something you have (phone, security key) or something you are (fingerprint). A stolen password alone is no longer enough.
why_it_matters: Strong password + MFA is generally much safer than a password alone, because the attacker also needs your device or key.
warning_signs: You receive an MFA prompt when you are not logging in.
You receive many prompts in a row ('MFA fatigue' - hoping you approve one to make them stop).
Someone calls or messages asking you to read out an MFA code.
A login page asks for your MFA code on a site you reached through an email link.
safe_practices: Only approve prompts you started yourself, and check the location/app shown.
Use number-matching or code-display prompts where available.
Prefer phishing-resistant methods: passkeys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) or hardware security keys.
Register backup methods and store recovery codes securely.
Never share one-time codes with anyone.
what_to_do: Deny any unexpected prompt.
Change your password - unexpected prompts often mean it is already known.
Report the prompts to the security team so they can check sign-in logs.

extra_sections.title: Phishing-resistant authentication and passkeys
items: Passkeys use public-key cryptography (WebAuthn/FIDO2). The private key never leaves your device.
A passkey is bound to the real website's domain, so it will not work on a look-alike phishing site.
There is no code to type, so there is nothing for a phisher to steal and replay.
SMS codes are better than no MFA, but are weaker than app-based or passkey methods.

title: Social Engineering
summary: Attackers manipulate trust, fear and helpfulness - verification defeats them.
what_is_it: Social engineering is manipulating people into breaking security procedures - by phone (vishing), SMS (smishing), chat, email or in person (tailgating).
why_it_matters: It bypasses technical controls entirely by targeting human instincts such as helpfulness, fear of authority and urgency.
warning_signs: A caller claims to be from IT, the bank or a senior manager and asks you to skip normal process.
Requests for gift cards, secrecy ('don't tell anyone') or unusual payments.
Pressure to act before you can check with anyone.
Someone without a badge asks you to hold the door to a secure area.
Messages that feel oddly personal, using details from social media.
safe_practices: Verify identity using a known number or directory - not the contact details provided by the requester.
Follow dual-approval rules for payments and bank-detail changes.
It is always OK to say 'I will call you back'.
Limit what you share publicly about your role and organisation.
Challenge politely or report unknown people in secure areas.
what_to_do: Stop the interaction and do not provide information.
Report the attempt with as many details as you remember (time, number, what was asked).
If you already shared information, tell the security team immediately.

title: Safe Browsing
summary: Browse deliberately: check addresses, keep browsers updated, avoid unofficial downloads.
what_is_it: Safe browsing is a set of habits that reduce the chance of landing on fake, compromised or malicious websites.
why_it_matters: Look-alike sites, malicious ads and compromised sites can steal credentials or deliver malware.
warning_signs: Misspelled or look-alike web addresses.
Pop-ups claiming your device is infected and urging you to call a number.
Sites demanding you install a 'codec', 'update' or extension to continue.
Browser certificate warnings on sites that normally work fine.
Download buttons that are actually adverts.
safe_practices: Keep your browser and extensions updated; remove extensions you do not use.
Download software only from official vendor sites or approved app stores.
Use bookmarks for important sites.
Remember: the padlock (HTTPS) means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is trustworthy.
Do not ignore certificate warnings.
what_to_do: Close the tab (use Task Manager if a pop-up will not close). Do not call numbers shown on scare pop-ups.
If you downloaded or ran something suspicious, disconnect from the network and report it.
Change passwords you entered on a suspicious site.

title: Secure Wi-Fi
summary: Treat public Wi-Fi as untrusted and protect your home network.
what_is_it: Wi-Fi security covers how you connect to wireless networks at home, at work and in public places.
why_it_matters: Open or fake hotspots can let others observe or redirect your traffic. Weak home routers can be taken over.
warning_signs: Open networks with generic names like 'Free_Airport_WiFi'.
Two networks with almost the same name (a possible 'evil twin').
Captive portals asking for unnecessary personal details or passwords.
Unexpected certificate warnings after connecting.
safe_practices: Use your organisation's VPN on public networks.
Prefer your phone's hotspot over unknown public Wi-Fi.
At home: use WPA3 (or WPA2-AES), a strong Wi-Fi password, and change the router's default admin password.
Keep router firmware updated.
Turn off auto-join for open networks.
what_to_do: Disconnect if something looks wrong.
Change passwords used while connected to a suspicious network.
Report suspicious office Wi-Fi networks to IT.

title: Software Updates & Patching
summary: Updates close the doors attackers already know about.
what_is_it: Updates (patches) fix security weaknesses (vulnerabilities) in operating systems, browsers, apps and devices.
why_it_matters: Many successful attacks use vulnerabilities for which a patch already exists. Delaying updates leaves known doors open.
warning_signs: Devices that have not restarted to install updates for weeks.
Software that is 'end of life' and no longer receives security fixes.
Update prompts that appear inside a web page rather than from the app or OS itself (a common trick).
safe_practices: Turn on automatic updates.
Restart when prompted so updates actually install.
Only update through the official app/OS mechanism.
Replace unsupported software and devices.
what_to_do: If an update fails repeatedly, contact IT.
If you suspect a fake update prompt, close it and report it.

title: Ransomware Awareness
summary: Ransomware locks or steals data for extortion; backups, patching and fast reporting limit the damage.
what_is_it: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts files and/or steals data, then demands payment. Many groups also threaten to publish stolen data ('double extortion').
why_it_matters: It can stop an entire organisation - hospitals, schools, factories - for days or weeks.
warning_signs: Files suddenly renamed with an unfamiliar extension or that will not open.
A ransom note on screen or in folders.
Very slow systems and unusual disk activity.
Security tools reporting blocked or quarantined files.
safe_practices: Report suspicious emails and attachments - they are a common entry point.
Keep devices patched and do not disable security tools.
Save work to approved, backed-up locations.
Use MFA - stolen remote-access passwords are another common entry point.
what_to_do: Disconnect the device from the network (unplug the cable / turn off Wi-Fi) but do not power it off unless told to - evidence in memory can help responders.
Report immediately to the security team or helpdesk.
Do not try to pay, negotiate or 'decrypt' anything yourself.
Follow the incident response team's instructions.

title: USB & Removable Media Safety
summary: Unknown USB devices can carry malware - never plug in what you found.
what_is_it: Removable media includes USB drives, external disks, SD cards and even USB cables/chargers that can contain hidden electronics.
why_it_matters: Malware can spread via USB, and lost unencrypted drives can leak sensitive data.
warning_signs: A USB drive 'found' in the car park or left at reception.
Unexpected USB gifts at events.
A device that opens a keyboard window or command prompt when connected.
safe_practices: Never plug in unknown devices - hand them to IT/security.
Use encrypted, organisation-approved drives for work data.
Prefer approved cloud sharing over USB where possible.
Use your own charger or a power-only adapter in public charging stations.
what_to_do: If you plugged in an unknown device, unplug it and report it immediately.
Report lost drives that contained work data.

title: Data Privacy
summary: Collect less, share carefully, and protect personal data you handle.
what_is_it: Data privacy is about handling personal information (names, IDs, health, financial data) lawfully, fairly and securely.
why_it_matters: Leaked personal data harms real people and can lead to regulatory penalties and loss of trust.
warning_signs: Requests for more personal data than a task needs.
Spreadsheets of personal data sent to personal email or unapproved apps.
Sharing links set to 'anyone with the link'.
Personal data pasted into unapproved AI tools or public sites.
safe_practices: Collect and keep only what you need (data minimisation).
Share with specific people using approved tools and least privilege.
Lock your screen when away.
Check recipients before sending.
Review app permissions and privacy settings regularly.
what_to_do: If data was sent to the wrong person or exposed, report it immediately - many laws have short notification deadlines.
Do not try to hide or quietly fix the mistake.

title: Mobile Security
summary: Your phone holds your email, MFA and banking - protect it like a laptop.
what_is_it: Mobile security covers phones and tablets: screen locks, updates, apps, permissions and messaging scams (smishing).
why_it_matters: A compromised or lost phone can expose email, MFA codes, photos and payment apps.
warning_signs: SMS about missed deliveries, tolls or bank problems with a link.
Apps asking for permissions unrelated to their purpose (a torch app wanting contacts).
Requests to install apps from outside the official store.
Unexpected battery drain or data use.
safe_practices: Use a strong screen lock and biometrics.
Install apps only from official stores and review permissions.
Keep the OS and apps updated.
Enable remote locate/wipe.
Do not click links in unexpected SMS - open the official app instead.
what_to_do: If your phone is lost, use remote lock/wipe and report it if it held work data.
If you clicked a suspicious link or installed a suspicious app, report it and follow IT guidance.

title: Remote Work Security
summary: Bring the office's security habits home.
what_is_it: Security practices for working from home, cafes or while travelling.
why_it_matters: Home networks, shared devices and public spaces create new risks for work data.
warning_signs: Family members using your work device.
Confidential calls in public spaces.
Work files saved to personal cloud storage.
safe_practices: Use the company VPN and approved collaboration tools.
Lock your screen and keep work devices for work only.
Use a privacy screen in public.
Keep your home router updated and secured.
what_to_do: Report lost/stolen devices immediately.
Report suspected compromise even outside office hours using the official channel.

title: Cloud Account Security
summary: Cloud accounts are only as safe as their sign-in and sharing settings.
what_is_it: Protecting accounts on cloud services (email, file sharing, SaaS apps, developer consoles).
why_it_matters: A single compromised cloud account can expose shared files, mailboxes and connected apps.
warning_signs: OAuth consent prompts asking a new app for broad access to your mailbox or files.
Sign-in alerts from unknown locations.
Files shared publicly by default.
Access keys or tokens committed to code repositories.
safe_practices: Use MFA/passkeys on all cloud accounts.
Review connected apps and remove unused ones.
Share with named people rather than public links.
Store secrets in a secrets manager or environment variables, never in code.
what_to_do: Revoke suspicious app access and sessions.
Rotate any exposed keys immediately.
Report the event to the security team.

title: Incident Reporting
summary: Report early, report everything suspicious - speed limits damage.
what_is_it: Incident reporting means quickly telling the security team about anything suspicious: messages, lost devices, odd system behaviour or mistakes.
why_it_matters: Early reports let responders contain problems before they spread. A report that turns out harmless is still useful.
warning_signs: You clicked a link or opened a file and something felt wrong.
You notice unusual account activity.
A device is lost or stolen.
Data was sent to the wrong person.
safe_practices: Know the official reporting channels (report button, helpdesk, security email/phone).
Include what happened, when, which device/account, and what you already did.
Do not investigate on your own or delete evidence.
Report even if you are unsure - nobody is punished for reporting in good faith.
what_to_do: Report immediately through the official channel.
Preserve evidence: do not delete emails or files.
Follow responders' instructions.

title: AI-Enabled Scam Awareness
summary: Voices, videos and messages can be convincingly faked - verify through a second channel.
what_is_it: Scammers use AI to write flawless messages, clone voices from short recordings and create deepfake videos to impersonate trusted people.
why_it_matters: Traditional red flags like bad grammar are disappearing; a familiar voice or face is no longer proof of identity.
warning_signs: A 'manager' or relative on a call or video urgently requesting money or secrets.
Slight audio/video glitches, unnatural pauses, or refusal to switch to a normal call.
Perfectly written but unusual requests that bypass normal process.
safe_practices: Verify through a second, known channel before acting on any money or data request.
Agree a verification phrase with family or team for emergencies.
Follow payment approval processes even for senior requests.
Limit public voice/video samples where practical.
what_to_do: Pause, end the call, and call back on a known number.
Report the attempt to the security team.
